 Hub: Streamers Up the Heat on Subscribers
 Erik Gruenwedel 
 November 11, 2026
 As streaming prices rise and free options expand, streaming services are feeling the heat.
 New data from Hub Entertainment Research Churn Tracker found that one in five survey respondents said they had canceled a SVOD service in the previous six months, with saving money the top reason.
 In the survey, 85% agreed that frequent price hikes make them feel taken advantage of, and 80% said higher prices push them to look for free alternatives. Only 16% said a price increase would cause them to cancel immediately, but a quarter said it would prompt them to actively shop for cheaper or free replacements.
 Over the past three months, Peacock, ESPN Unlimited, Apple TV, and Disney all announced price increases. Those moves followed earlier hikes from Netflix and Prime in March. The steady climb has been underway for years. Peacock’s ad-supported premium tier, for example, has more than doubled from $5.99 a month in July 2023 to $12.99 today.
 The increases are not random. Streamers are using higher prices on premium plans to nudge customers toward ad-supported tiers that generate extra advertising revenue and toward multi-service bundles that tend to have lower cancellation rates.
 Disney raised prices across nearly all of its packages while holding the price of its ad-supported Disney+/Hulu bundle steady. For many households, however, the practical result is a higher monthly bill at a time when budgets are already tight.
 Consumer finances are under pressure. The University of Michigan’s consumer sentiment index fell to its second-lowest level on record in October, down 13.6% from a year earlier. Personal savings rates have continued to decline even as credit-card debt rises.
 Inflation stood at 3.7% year over year in September, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics — the sixth straight month that price increases outpaced wage growth. With purchasing power eroding, households are less willing to absorb another round of subscription increases without resistance.
 The longer-term challenge for paid streaming is abundant free entertainment on YouTube, ad-supported video-on-demand services, and social media.
 Nielsen data shows that YouTube and The Roku Channel gained market share faster than any other streaming platforms over the past year. YouTube’s growth alone exceeded the combined gains of the major paid subscription services.
 The pattern resembles the cable television industry in the 2010s. Cable was still near its peak when Netflix and other streamers began attracting younger viewers. Providers continued raising prices. Cord-cutting started gradually and then accelerated, and by the late 2010s the traditional cable model was in deep trouble.
 “For now, many subscribers remain,” wrote analyst Ed Isabella in a post. “How long that lasts will depend on whether platforms can slow the rate of increases, improve the value of their bundles, or find other ways to keep customers from noticing the water is getting hotter.”
